d: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — four properties guaranteeing reliable processing of database transactions.

In domain_driven_design, an aggregate is a cluster of related entities and value_objects treated as a single unit for data changes; the aggregate_root is the single entity within that cluster that external objects reference and interact with, enforcing invariants and encapsulating the aggregate's internal state.
An integration pattern where a service calls multiple backend services and combines their responses into a single result for the client.
A helper service that offloads client-side network responsibilities (retry, circuit_breaker, monitoring) from the application into a sidecar container.
A commonly used pattern that appears beneficial but is actually counterproductive; architectural anti_patterns include big_ball_of_mud, golden_hammer, and spaghetti_code.

A pattern where a facade or aggregation layer combines data from multiple backend services or APIs into a single unified response, enabling clients to retrieve consolidated results without managing multiple round-trips or service contracts.
A server entry point that routes requests to backend services, handling cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate_limiting, and protocol_translation.
Application Performance Monitoring — tooling that provides observability into application performance through metrics, tracing, and profiling.
Automatically adjusting the number of compute instances based on demand metrics (CPU, request_count, queue_depth), improving resource efficiency.

In distributed_systems and reliability engineering, availability is the proportion of time a system remains operational and accessible, often expressed as a percentage (e.g., 99.99%) over a measurement window.
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — a consistency model used by distributed systems (especially NoSQL) that trades strict consistency for availability.
An anti_pattern describing a system whose architecture has deteriorated into an entangled, inseparable mass, making changes risky and difficult.
A pattern where multiple specialized knowledge sources contribute to a shared knowledge base (the blackboard), which is read and updated by a control component. Common in AI systems.
A deployment strategy maintaining two identical production environments (blue and green), switching traffic atomically to the new version after validation.
In domain_driven_design, a boundary within which a particular domain_model is defined and applicable, separating it from other contexts where the same terms may have different meanings.
A resilience pattern that isolates resources (threads, connections, partitions) so that failure in one partition does not affect others, named after ship bulkheads.
Approaches for storing frequently accessed data closer to consumers (CDN, in_memory_cache, distributed_cache) to reduce latency and backend load.
A deployment strategy where a new version is released to a small subset of users first, gradually increasing traffic as confidence grows.
Context-Driven Delivery — an architectural approach where decisions are made based on the specific context and tradeoffs rather than applying patterns prescriptively.
The practice of deliberately introducing failures into a system in a controlled manner to identify weaknesses and improve resilience before failures occur in production.
A distributed coordination pattern where services exchange events without a central orchestrator; each service knows what to do based on received events.
A resilience pattern that wraps calls to a remote service and trips open when failures exceed a threshold, preventing cascading failures by failing fast.
A pattern for handling large messages by storing the payload in an external store (blob_storage, data_lake) and passing only a reference (claim_check) through the message bus.

An architectural pattern proposed by Robert Martin that structures software into concentric layers (entities, use_cases, interface_adapters, frameworks_drivers) with strict dependency rules pointing inward.
A distributed model where a client requests services from a server, which provides resources or computations. The server may be stateless or maintain session_state.
The degree to which elements inside a module belong together; high cohesion indicates that a module's responsibilities form a meaningful unit, improving maintainability.
An architecture style that emphasizes separation of concerns and reuse through discrete, independently replaceable software components, each encapsulating a specific functionality.
Packaging an application with its dependencies into a container_image for consistent deployment across environments, with Docker being the dominant implementation.
A testing approach that verifies the contracts between services (API schemas, message formats) independently, ensuring compatibility without end_to_end_testing.
The degree of interdependence between software modules; high coupling means modules are heavily dependent on each other, while low (loose) coupling is a design goal.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation — a pattern that separates read (query) and write (command) operations into different models, allowing independent optimization of each path.
Conflict-free Replicated Data Types — data structures that can be merged automatically across distributed nodes without coordination, enabling conflict-free eventual_consistency.
A storage repository that holds vast amounts of raw data in its native format until needed, supporting diverse analytics and machine_learning workloads.
A centralized repository for integrated data from multiple sources, optimized for analytical queries and business_intelligence workloads.
A data management pattern in microservices where each service owns and manages its own database schema or instance, enforcing loose coupling.
A message queue destination for messages that cannot be processed successfully, allowing investigation and reprocessing without losing failed messages.
A SOLID principle stating that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete implementations.

A cache shared across multiple nodes or processes in a distributed_system, providing low-latency access to frequently used data by storing it in memory across the cluster rather than fetching from a central database.
Tracking a request as it flows through multiple services by propagating correlation_ids, enabling end-to-end visibility into latency sources and failure points.

A transaction that spans multiple independent services or database_per_service instances, requiring coordination to maintain atomicity across nodes where each participant may reside in a different process or machine.

A software development approach that focuses on modeling software based on the real-world domain, using bounded_contexts, entities, value_objects, aggregates, and a ubiquitous_language shared between domain experts and developers.

database_per_service is a data management pattern in microservices where each service owns and manages its own database schema or instance, enforcing loose coupling between services through physical data isolation.
schema_isolation means each service's database exposes only the data and operations relevant to its bounded context, hiding internal structures from other services.

instance_isolation means each service runs its own database server process or cluster, with separate credentials, ports, and storage, preventing any service from accessing another's data store directly.
polyglot_persistence is the practice where different services within the same system use different database technologies (SQL, NoSQL, graph, etc.) best suited to each service's data model.
schema_ownership declares that a service is the sole authority for defining, migrating, and evolving its database schema; no other service may modify it.
data_duplication is the consequence of database_per_service where the same logical entity may be materialized in multiple service databases, kept synchronized through application-level events.

api_composition is the pattern where a client or gateway aggregates data from multiple service databases by querying each service's API and combining results, compensating for the lack of cross-service SQL joins.

cqrs_boundary applies within a single service's database where command operations (writes) and query operations (reads) against the same logical entity use separate data representations, all contained within that service's schema.

migration_orchestration is the process of evolving a service's schema independently, typically done via versioned migration scripts (e.g., Flyway, Liquibase) that each service applies on its own schedule.
connection_pool_per_service means each service manages its own database connection pool, sized independently based on that service's concurrency needs.
backup_and_recovery_scope defines that each service backs up and restores only its own database, making recovery operations independent across services.
service_catalog_entry is the registration of a service's database connection metadata (host, port, credentials ref) in a service_discovery registry, so authorized services or operators can locate it.
database_as_sidecar deploys a database container alongside a service container, such that the database is co-located, co-scoped, and co-lifecycled with that specific service.

eventual_consistency_model is the consistency guarantee that results from database_per_service: writes are immediately durable in one service's database, and other services receive updates asynchronously via event_streaming or message_queue.
shared_nothing_architecture is the architectural property that database_per_service embodies: no shared disk, no shared schema, no shared connection pool across service boundaries.
bounded_context_enforcement is the enforcement of domain-driven design bounded contexts through database_per_service, where each context's canonical model is stored only in its own database.
Don't Repeat Yourself — a principle advocating for single-source-of-truth in code to avoid duplication and the maintenance nightmares it creates.
An anti_pattern where an application simultaneously writes to two systems (e.g., database and message broker) without transactional guarantees, risking inconsistency.
A named set of event consumers that share progress tracking across partitions; the broker ensures each partition is assigned to exactly one member within the group for load-balanced consumption.
An entity that reads events sequentially from a stream partition, maintaining its own offset position and processing events independently of other consumers.
An ordered, independent, immutable segment of an event stream; events within a partition maintain strict ordering; partitions enable parallelism and throughput scaling.
An entity that serializes and writes events to a stream topic, optionally routing to specific partitions based on key hashing or explicit partition assignment.

An immutable entry appended to the event log consisting of a key, value payload, timestamp, headers, and a per-partition offset; once written it is never modified or deleted except by retention policy.

An immutable, append-only log of events organized in time-order, retained for a configurable duration or size, enabling multiple independent consumers to read from any position and replay historical events.
A mandatory timestamp attribute on each event record indicating when the event occurred (event time) or when it was ingested (processing time), enabling temporal ordering and windowing.
A retention mechanism that retains only the most recent event per key within each partition, enabling compacted streams to serve as key-value changelogs while reclaiming storage.

An optional routing key on an event record used by producers to determine target partition via consistent hashing, ensuring events with the same key land in the same partition for ordering guarantees.
A configuration defining time-based (e.g., 7 days) or size-based (e.g., 10GB per partition) boundaries that determine when older events are purged from the log.
A centralized service managing versioned schemas (Avro, Protobuf, JSON Schema) for event payloads; producers validate against registered schemas and consumers deserialize accordingly.
The streaming platform intermediary (e.g., Kafka broker, Pulsar) that persists events durably to disk, manages partitions, and serves consumer reads at scale.
A monotonically increasing integer position marker within a partition that uniquely identifies an event record; consumers commit offsets to enable resume-from-failure semantics.
The capability for a consumer to reset its committed offset backward and re-read historical events from a partition, enabling reprocessing, debugging, and new consumer bootstrapping.
Extract, Transform, Load — a data integration process that extracts data from sources, transforms it for analysis, and loads it into a destination.
A software design pattern where the flow of the program is determined by events (user actions, sensor outputs, messages) and the propagation of events through the system.
A pattern where the state of an application is stored as a sequence of events rather than current state. The event_log becomes the source of truth; state is reconstructed by replaying events.

An immutable, append-only ordered log of events retained over time, enabling multiple independent consumers to read from any position; unlike ephemeral pub/sub messages, events persist for a configurable retention window and can be replayed.
A data handling approach where events are captured in order as an immutable log (stream), allowing multiple consumers to read independently (e.g., Kafka, Pulsar).
A consistency model where updates propagate through a distributed system asynchronously; given enough time without new updates, all replicas will converge to the same value.
A system quality attribute measuring how easily new functionality can be added without modifying existing code (open_closed_principle in practice).
A resilience pattern that provides an alternative response or behavior when the primary service call fails, improving user experience.
A pattern where an API_gateway routes requests to appropriate backend services based on request characteristics (URL path, headers) without the client knowing service locations.
Integration with load_balancing to distribute requests across multiple instances of a backend service.
A microservice or backend resource that receives forwarded requests from the gateway.
Integration with circuit_breaker logic to prevent routing to failing backend services.
A predefined route or behavior triggered when primary routing fails or no route matches.
A matching rule based on request or response header values for routing decisions.
The addition, removal, or modification of HTTP headers during request forwarding.
A routing constraint based on HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) for route matching.
A URL path template or pattern used to match incoming request paths for routing decisions.
A transformation that modifies the request path before forwarding to the backend service.
A component that evaluates incoming requests against route matching criteria.
The combination of responses from multiple backend services into a single client response.
The mechanism that forwards matched requests to backend services and returns responses to clients.
A defined mapping between incoming request criteria and a target backend service endpoint.
The declarative or imperative specification of a route including matching criteria and target service.
The ordering rule that determines which route takes precedence when multiple routes match.
Integration with service_discovery to dynamically resolve backend service network locations.
An anti_pattern where a familiar tool or solution is overapplied to problems it was not designed for, ignoring better alternatives.
An API query language and runtime where clients specify exactly what data they need, as an alternative to REST's fixed response structures.
A high-performance, open-source RPC framework using HTTP/2 for transport and Protocol Buffers for serialization, enabling strict contracts between services.
An interface endpoint that reports whether a service instance is functioning correctly and ready to receive traffic, used by load_balancers and orchestrators.

An architectural pattern (ports_and_adapters) that structures the application with a core business logic at the center, surrounded by ports for input and output adapters, keeping the core independent of external concerns.

A design principle where elements within a module, class, or component are strongly related and serve a single purpose; high cohesion within modules complements loose_coupling between them, improving maintainability and clarity.
Scaling out by adding more machines to a system, as opposed to vertical_scaling which adds resources to existing machines.

A binary wire protocol succeeding HTTP/1.1 that multiplexes multiple concurrent requests over a single TCP connection, supports header compression, and enables bidirectional server push, serving as the transport layer for grpc_architecture.

The stateless request-response application protocol underlying the web, defining methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) for manipulating resources identified by URIs, upon which restful_architecture builds its uniform_interface constraints.
An infrastructure management approach where servers are never modified after deployment; changes require creating new instances, improving consistency and rollback.

A simplification of lambda_architecture that uses a single streaming layer (typically Apache Kafka) for both real-time and historical processing, avoiding the complexity of maintaining separate batch and speed layers.
Keep It Simple, Stupid — a design principle advocating for simplicity in system design and avoiding unnecessary complexity.
A container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications across clusters of machines.
A data processing architecture that combines batch and stream (speed) processing layers using a serving_layer for queries, designed for systems where both historical and real-time data are needed.
A design guideline stating that an object should only communicate with its immediate collaborators, not with objects obtained through those collaborators, reducing coupling.

A software architecture pattern that organizes code into horizontal layers, each with a specific responsibility (e.g., presentation, business logic, data access). Higher layers depend on lower layers; dependency flow is unidirectional.
A technique for distributing network traffic or workload across multiple servers to ensure no single resource is overwhelmed, improving responsiveness and availability.
The practice of recording application events, errors, and audit trails to persistent storage for debugging, monitoring, and compliance purposes.

A design property where modules or services minimize their dependencies on each other, interacting through well-defined interfaces or abstractions so that changes to one component do not require changes in others.
A system quality attribute measuring how easily the system can be modified to correct defects, improve performance, or adapt to new requirements.
A precomputed query result stored as a table, updated asynchronously to provide fast read access to complex query results.
An integration pattern where system components communicate via a shared message_bus (ESB), which handles routing, transformation, and delivery of messages between services.
A communication mechanism where messages are placed in a queue by producers and consumed asynchronously by consumers, decoupling sender and receiver in time and space.
Quantitative measurements of system behavior (CPU_usage, request_latency, error_rate) collected and aggregated for monitoring and alerting.

An architecture with a minimal core (kernel) providing basic OS services, with extended functionality provided by modular plugins or servers. In software, the core handles essential operations while plugins handle specialized features.

An architectural style that structures an application as a collection of small, autonomous, loosely-coupled services organized around business capabilities, each deployable independently and communicating via lightweight protocols.
A software deployment model where all components (UI, business logic, data access) are packaged and deployed as a single unit. The opposite of distributed architectures.
A distributed coordination pattern where a central coordinator (orchestrator) directs the flow of operations across services, contrasting with choreography.
A reliability pattern for distributed systems where a database outbox table stores pending events alongside business transactions; a relay process publishes these events reliably.
A decentralized architecture where nodes (peers) act as both clients and servers, sharing resources directly without requiring a central coordination point.
A structural pattern where data flows through a series of processing components (filters) connected by pipes. Each filter processes input and produces output for the next stage.

An architectural style where a minimal core system exposes extension points that allow modules (plugins) to be loaded dynamically at runtime, enabling feature extensibility without modifying the core, as employed by microkernel_architecture.

An architectural pattern that separates the core business logic from external concerns by defining ports (interfaces) for inputs and outputs, with adapters implementing those ports to connect to frameworks, databases, or external systems.
An architectural pattern where a surrogate object acts as an interface to another object, adding behavior like lazy_initialization, access_control, or logging.
A delivery mode where a single message published to a topic is forwarded to all current subscribers of that topic without modification.
An alias or alternative naming for a topic within the broker's namespace, representing the logical path between publishers and subscribers.
A holding area for messages that failed delivery after repeated retry attempts, enabling later inspection and reprocessing without losing event data.
The structured wrapper around a message containing metadata such as timestamp, source identifier, and routing attributes used by the broker for delivery decisions.
A routing behavior where a single published message results in independent delivery copies to each subscriber, allowing individual acknowledgment without affecting other recipients.
The event payload or notification transmitted by a publisher through a topic to all interested subscribers.
The middleware infrastructure component that hosts topics, receives published messages, and routes them to the appropriate subscriber queues.
A predicate or selector expression applied to message content or headers that determines whether a given subscriber receives a particular message on a topic.
An event source that produces messages and emits them to one or more topics without knowledge of downstream subscribers or their identities.
An event consumer that registers interest in one or more topics and receives messages routed to those topics without knowledge of upstream publishers.
The registered interest record binding a specific subscriber to a specific topic, enabling the broker to know where to route matching messages.
A named routing channel or subject that publishers send messages to and that subscribers listen on for filtered delivery of those messages.
The operation by which a subscriber revokes its registered interest in a topic, ceasing further message delivery for that topic.
A messaging pattern where publishers send messages to a topic without knowing subscribers, and subscribers receive messages published to topics they are interested in.
The intermediary component that receives messages from publishers and forwards them to subscribers based on topic subscriptions; may also perform filtering.
A predicate or attribute-based rule applied at the broker or subscriber side to select a subset of messages on a topic for delivery.
A destination for messages that cannot be successfully delivered to any subscriber, capturing failures for later inspection or replay.
The payload broadcast by a publisher on a topic; in pub/sub it is typically ephemeral and not persisted beyond active subscriber consumption.
A structured format (JSON, Avro, Protobuf) defining the shape of messages on a topic, enabling subscribers to deserialize and interpret published events.
An entity that sends messages to a topic without knowing which subscribers will receive them; decoupled from consumers in both space and time.
An entity that expresses interest in one or more topics and receives messages published to those topics; receives only messages matching its subscriptions.
An active registration linking a subscriber to a topic; may be durable (surviving subscriber disconnection) or transient (active only while subscriber is connected).
A named channel or subject through which messages are routed from publishers to interested subscribers; the publisher has no knowledge of subscriber identities or count.
A hierarchical or scoped naming scheme for topics (e.g., orders.new, orders.cancelled) that enables subscribers to express interest at varying levels of granularity.
A traffic_management technique that controls how many requests a client can make in a given time period, protecting services from overload and abuse.
A database replica optimized for read operations, offloading read traffic from the primary database and improving query performance.
A system quality attribute measuring the probability that the system performs its intended function correctly under designated conditions for a specified period.

A category of fault_tolerance patterns (including circuit_breaker_pattern, retry_pattern, bulkhead_pattern, and fallback_pattern) that enable a distributed_system to continue operating gracefully when components fail or degrade.
An architectural style using HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resources identified by URIs, following stateless communication, cacheability, and uniform_interface constraints.
A resilience pattern that automatically retries failed operations with configurable backoff strategies to handle transient failures.
A deployment strategy that incrementally replaces instances of the old version with the new one, maintaining availability throughout the update.
A pattern for managing distributed transactions across microservices using a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions for rollback, replacing distributed transactions.
A system quality attribute measuring its ability to handle increased load (users, requests, data volume) by scaling up (vertical) or scaling out (horizontal).
A messaging pattern where a request is broadcast to multiple recipients (scatter) and responses are collected and aggregated (gather) to produce a final result.
A design principle that states each module or layer should have responsibility over a single aspect of the software's functionality, reducing coupling between concerns.
An architectural pattern where application logic runs in stateless compute containers managed by a cloud_provider (e.g., AWS Lambda, Azure Functions), abstracting server management entirely.
The automatic detection of services and their network locations (IP address, port) in a dynamic infrastructure, typically via client_side_discovery or server_side_discovery.

A dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service_to_service communication, providing observability, traffic_management, and security without embedding this logic in application code (e.g., Istio, Linkerd).

An architectural pattern where application components provide services to other components via a communication protocol, typically over a network. SOA emphasizes interoperability and composition of services.
A data partitioning strategy where data is distributed across database shards based on a shard_key, enabling horizontal scaling of data storage.
An anti_pattern in microservices where multiple services share the same database, creating tight coupling and hindering independent deployment.
A deployment pattern where a helper container (sidecar) is attached to a main application container to extend or add functionality without modifying the application.
A SOLID principle stating that a class or module should have only one reason to change, embodying the idea that each component should have one job.
Five object-oriented design principles (single_responsibility, open_closed, liskov_substitution, interface_segregation, dependency_inversion) that guide maintainable software design.

An architecture designed for high concurrency and scalability by using a shared memory space (tuple_space or distributed_cache) instead of a traditional database, eliminating synchronization bottlenecks.
An anti_pattern where code has little to no structure, with complex and tangled control flow, making it nearly impossible to maintain or extend.
A migration strategy where a new system gradually replaces an old system by incrementally routing functionality, eventually strangling the legacy system.
A flow control mechanism by which a slow consumer signals producers or the broker to pause delivery, preventing unbounded buffer growth and consumer overwhelm under burst load.

A durable record of a consumer's committed offset position in a partition, persisted outside the stream itself, enabling fault-tolerant resumption from the last acknowledged event after process failure.

A retention policy variant that retains only the latest event per message key within a log, discarding older superseded events with the same key while preserving the full event history for keys not yet updated.
An entity that reads events from one or more stream partitions independently, maintaining its own offset cursor; multiple consumers may read the same partition concurrently without coordination.
A named set of stream consumers sharing the work of consuming a topic, where each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group to prevent duplicate processing.
The numerical difference between the latest offset written to a partition and the offset last committed by a consumer, indicating how far behind real-time the consumer is and often used for alerting.

The guaranteed level of event delivery a streaming system provides to consumers: at-least-once (events may be redelivered), at-most-once (events may be dropped), or exactly-once (each event is processed precisely one time end-to-end).

An immutable record appended to an event stream, containing a payload (message body), a timestamp, a partition key, and an offset; once written it is never modified, only retained or expired according to retention policy.

The numeric difference between the latest stream_offset produced and the last offset consumed by a stream_consumer or stream_consumer_group; measures how far behind the consumer is and serves as a primary operational metric for stream health.

An immutable append-only sequence of events retained on disk or equivalent durable storage; unlike pubsub_message which is ephemeral, events in a stream_log persist for the configured retention period and can be reread from any offset by any consumer group.

A structured definition (often expressed in Avro, Protocol Buffers, or JSON Schema) that describes the fields, types, and layout of messages flowing through an event_streaming or message_queue system, enabling producers and consumers to serialize and deserialize events consistently.

A monotonically increasing integer position marker assigned to each event within a partition, uniquely identifying the event's place in the partition's sequence and enabling consumers to resume reading from a specific point.

A distinct, ordered slice of an event stream, identified by a partition key or index, enabling parallel production and consumption; each partition maintains its own offset sequence independently of other partitions.

A stateful or stateless transform that reads events from a stream, applies computation or enrichment, and optionally writes derived events to an output stream; may maintain local or distributed state.
An entity that writes events to a stream partition, optionally selecting the partition via a keying function; producers are typically decoupled from consumers and do not track subscriber state.

The capability to re-read events from a stream_log starting at any prior stream_offset or timestamp; enabled by durable retention, replay allows new consumers or recovering systems to reprocess historical events without re-producing them.
The number of redundant copies of each partition maintained across distinct brokers or nodes, providing fault tolerance against broker failures and enabling continued consumption during outages.
The configured duration or size limit after which events are automatically discarded from a stream partition; governs how far back consumers can replay and the storage cost bound.
A centralized service that stores and manages schemas for stream events, enforcing compatibility constraints on schema evolution and enabling consumers to deserialize events correctly.
A durable key-value store maintained by a stream processor to hold intermediate or accumulated state, backed by the event stream and checkpointed for fault-tolerant recovery.
An association linking a pubsub_topic in the relative root to one or more stream partitions, describing how publish/subscribe channels are realized as persisted streams.

A timestamp marking the earliest point in time for which all events have been fully ingested into a partition, used by windowed stream processors to determine when to emit results for time-based windows.

A temporal or session-based grouping of consecutive events within a partition, defined by fixed time intervals, sliding parameters, or session inactivity gaps, over which aggregations or joins are computed.
The implied cost of additional rework caused by choosing a quick and easy solution now instead of a better approach that would take longer.
A system quality attribute measuring how easily and effectively software components can be tested in isolation.
A flow_control mechanism that limits the rate of operations (API calls, message processing) to prevent resource exhaustion.
A pattern combining a database transaction with an outbox_table to atomically persist state changes and event records, eliminating the need for dual_writes.
A distributed transaction protocol with a prepare phase (where all participants vote) and a commit phase (where coordinator directs all to commit or abort), ensuring atomicity across nodes.
In domain_driven_design, a shared language between development team and domain experts that is consistently used in code, conversations, and documentation within a bounded_context.
Scaling up by adding more CPU, RAM, or storage to existing machines, as opposed to horizontal_scaling which adds more machines.
A distributed pattern where work items are placed in a queue and consumed by available workers, enabling asynchronous processing and load distribution.
You Aren't Gonna Need It — an extreme programming principle that advises against adding functionality until it is actually needed.
